title: Where Were You?
sum: After thirty-five chapters of argument, the LORD himself answers Job from a windstorm. He does not explain the wager with the Accuser, accuse Job of hidden sins, or defend the friends. Instead he asks questions: "Where were you when I founded the earth?" He takes Job on a tour of the world, from its foundations and the birth of the sea to dawn, death, snow, rain, stars and lightning.

Then the tour turns to the animals: the lion and the raven, fed by God. The questions are not a quiz. They show Job a world far larger than his case, full of order and wildness, most of it with no human in it at all, all of it known to God. Rain falls "on a desert where no person lives" (38:26). Job had asked for a verdict; he is given a view.
readings: Read as rebuke

God puts Job in his place. Job spoke beyond his knowledge (38:2), and the flood of questions shows how little a human can grasp. This is the most common reading in Jewish and Christian tradition, and it explains Job's silence in 40:4–5 and his retraction in 42:6.
Read as consolation

The questions open Job's eyes to a world of beauty and care. God shapes the dawn, feeds raven chicks and wraps the sea like a newborn. A God who tends ibex in labor has not forgotten Job. Readers such as Andersen and Hartley stress that God came at all: the answer is the meeting.
Read as a new picture of the world

Job and his friends assumed the world was built to reward and punish humans. God shows a creation with its own purposes, where rain falls on empty land and predators are fed. Justice is real (38:13–15), but the world is not a courtroom. Newsom, Alter and others read the speech this way.

views.H: Readers who take Job as history understand that God really spoke from a storm, as at Sinai. Many add that the speech was put into the poetic form we have by the inspired author, as speeches in ancient histories were.
views.C: Most critics take the divine speeches as the poet's climax, written by the same hand as the dialogue, though some older scholars thought they were added. The speech is carefully built: cosmos (38:4–38), then animals (38:39–39:30), with five pairs of creatures in the second half. No Hebrew manuscript from Qumran survives for chapters 38–42 (the published 4QJob fragments stop in chapter 37), but the Aramaic Targum from Cave 11 (11QtgJob) covers parts of these chapters; it is cited here at 42:6 and 42:11.
views.W: Ancient Near Eastern scribes made lists of everything in the world, such as the Egyptian Onomasticon of Amenope, and Gerhard von Rad argued that 38 draws on that list-making wisdom. Egyptian satirical letters (Papyrus Anastasi I) also test a scribe with a string of questions. But no ancient text answers a sufferer with a tour of creation like this one.
views.J: Jewish readers note that God answers Job "from the windstorm": the Talmud (Bava Batra 16a) puns that Job had complained that God bruises him in a windstorm (9:17), and God answers him with one. Maimonides (Guide 3.23) reads the speech as teaching that God's knowledge and providence are not like ours at all, which is the lesson Job had to learn. The morning blessing for the rooster's understanding comes from 38:36.
views.X: Christian readers have used this chapter to praise God the Creator and to warn against pride of mind. Gregory the Great reads it allegorically, finding the church, its teachers and its enemies in its images. Calvin preached through it, stressing that God's ways exceed our grasp. In the modern creation debate, "Where were you?" is quoted by young-earth creationists to argue against trusting scientific dating (see the card below); others reply that the chapter's picture of the world is poetic and ancient, and it is not trying to date creation.

deep.b: In chapter 3 Job cursed the day he was born. He called for darkness and deep shadow to take it (3:5), for its stars to go dark and for it never to see "the eyelids of dawn" (3:9), and for those "ready to wake Leviathan" to curse it (3:8). Robert Alter and others have shown that God's speeches answer that poem image by image. God speaks of light and darkness each in its place (38:12–20), of the morning stars singing (38:7), of the dawn shaking out the wicked (38:13), of deep shadow's gates (38:17), and finally of Leviathan, whose eyes "are like the eyelids of dawn" (41:18). Job wanted to undo creation for one day. God answers with the whole of creation, including the chaos Job wanted to call up, and says that it is his.

The speech is almost entirely questions, more than fifty in chapters 38–39. Some are sarcastic (38:5, 21), some are tender (38:41; 39:1–4). None is answered, and God does not expect answers. Ancient teachers often taught by questions, and the questions here move Job from speaker to listener. Job had said, "Then you call me, and I will answer. Or I will speak, and you give me a reply" (13:22). God does call, and Job finds he has nothing to say (40:4–5).

What God does not say is also striking. He never mentions the Accuser, Job's sins, or the reasons for the suffering. Readers have taken that silence as a lesson (the reasons are beyond Job), as mercy (God does not shame Job with the wager), or as a problem (Job is never told).

echoes: Genesis 1:1–2:3; Psalm 104; Proverbs 8:22–31; Psalm 147:9; Isaiah 40:12–14; Jeremiah 5:22; Amos 5:8; 9:9; 26:7–14; 3:3–10; Matthew 6:26; Luke 12:24; Romans 11:33–35

settings.what: The LORD's first speech from the storm
settings.by: The LORD (YHWH), speaking from a windstorm
settings.to: Job, sitting in his misery; the three friends (and Elihu) are presumably present, since God addresses Eliphaz in 42:7, but the speech is to Job alone
settings.when: Right after Elihu's last speech (37), and after Job had signed his oath of innocence and challenged God to answer (31:35–37)
settings.why: God accepts Job's challenge to a hearing, but changes its terms. Instead of answering charges, he questions Job about the making and running of the world, from the foundations to the wild animals. The speech is meant to make Job see what he does not know, and to show him a God whose care and power reach far beyond the human courtroom. Knowing it is spoken to Job, not to the friends, matters: it does not confirm their claim that Job is guilty.
settings.readers: Israelites in the exile or after it (the setting most scholars favor; the book's opening pages give the other datings), who had lost land, Temple and children, heard God speak of a world far larger than their disaster. The speech offered them no explanation for their losses, but a God who still governed sea, sky and desert and fed even the raven. It told them that the old formula of reward and punishment did not exhaust God's ways, and that God would meet the one who complained to his face.
views: God corrects Job's ignorance and pride (Jewish and Christian tradition generally; Calvin; Andersen in part).
The answer is God's presence and care, not an argument (Hartley; many devotional readers).
God replaces the human-centered moral world of the debate with a wider creation (Newsom, Alter, Habel).
Some modern readers (for example Curtis) hear God overpowering Job instead of answering him.

traditions.q: Does God's "Where were you when I founded the earth?" bear on how old the earth is?
views: No fixed teaching on the earth's age. The Church holds that faith and science cannot truly conflict and that Scripture teaches without error the truth God wanted put there for our salvation (Catechism 159, 283; Vatican II, Dei Verbum 11); the chapter teaches humility before the Creator.

No official ruling. Orthodox teachers stress the Fathers' reading of creation as God's free act and the theological meaning of the days; some modern Orthodox writers hold a young earth, many accept scientific dating.

Divided. The Westminster Confession says God made the world "in the space of six days" (4.1). Some Reformed scholars read the days literally and the earth as young; others (for example B. B. Warfield and many in the Presbyterian Church in America's 2000 creation report) allow an old earth. Job 38 is read as poetry about God's power on all sides.

The church teaches a recent creation in six literal days (Seventh-day Adventist Fundamental Belief 6), tied to the Sabbath; texts like Job 38 are read as confirming that God, not chance or long ages, made the world.

Divided. Young-earth creationists (Answers in Genesis, Henry Morris) use "Where were you?" to argue that no one but God saw the beginning, so his word outranks scientific dating; old-earth and evolutionary creationists (BioLogos, Hugh Ross) answer that the verse humbles all human claims, including theirs, and does not address dating.

title: The Wild Ones
sum: The tour of the animals continues. God asks whether Job knows when the ibex give birth, who set the wild donkey free, whether the wild ox will plow his field. He describes the foolish ostrich, which leaves its eggs in the dirt and yet outruns a horse; the war horse, which laughs at fear and cannot keep still when the ram's horn blows; and the hawk and eagle, which nest on the cliffs and feed their chicks on blood.

Almost every creature here lives outside human control and use. Several laugh at people. God knows and governs them all, delights in their strength and freedom, and does not apologize for the hard parts of nature. The first speech ends where the bodies lie, with an eagle on the battlefield.
readings: Read as God's care
God tends the births of animals no shepherd watches, gives the wild donkey its freedom and the eagle its nest. If he cares for these, he cares for Job (compare Matthew 6:26).
Read as wildness
These creatures cannot be tamed, used or understood by humans. The world is not a farm run for people. God's pleasure in them shows a creation with value of its own, comic, fierce and free.
Read as a mirror

Some readers see Job in the animals: like the wild donkey he is free, like the ostrich he has lost his young, like the horse he charges into battle (with God). The text does not draw the comparisons, but they are easy to feel.

views.H: Readers who take Job as history note the accurate observation of animals of the desert and steppe of the Near East: the ibex calving in secret, the onager on the salt flats, the aurochs, the ostrich's ground nest.
views.C: Critics note that the ostrich passage (39:13–18) differs in style, speaks of God in the third person, and was missing from the Old Greek; some take it as an addition, others as an intentional change of pace. The ten creatures of 38:39–39:30 are arranged in pairs.
views.W: Ancient kings showed their power by hunting lions and wild oxen (Assyrian palace reliefs) and by keeping exotic animals. Egyptian art pictures the "Lord of the Animals" holding beasts in each hand. God speaks here as the true Master of Animals, whose rule includes what humans cannot master.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition finds God's care for animal births in this chapter. The Talmud (Bava Batra 16a–b) says that the ibex (ya'alah) is cruel to her young, and when she crouches to give birth God sends an eagle to catch the kid as it falls; and that the hind (ayyalah) has a narrow womb, and God sends a serpent to bite it open at the right moment. God says: I do not confuse one moment with another; would I confuse Iyyov (Job) with oyev (enemy)?
views.X: Christian readers often moralized the animals: Gregory the Great reads, for example, the wild donkey as the hermit who flees the world, the ostrich as the hypocrite, the war horse as the preacher. Modern Christian writers on creation care (for example Bill McKibben, The Comforting Whirlwind) cite the chapter for God's love of wild creatures.

echoes: Psalm 104:10–30; Psalm 147:9; Genesis 16:12; Numbers 23:22; Deuteronomy 33:17; Lamentations 4:3; Jeremiah 8:7; Matthew 24:28; Luke 17:37; Isaiah 40:31

title: Behemoth
sum: God ends his first speech with a challenge: will the critic take the Almighty to court? Job answers briefly. He is a lightweight; he puts his hand over his mouth; he has spoken and will say no more. It is silence, not yet surrender, and God speaks again from the storm.

The second speech goes to the heart of the matter: "Would you declare me guilty so that you come out innocent?" (40:8). God invites Job to put on royal robes and bring down every proud and wicked person, if he can. Then he points to Behemoth, a huge grass-eating beast of the river marsh, "the first of the ways of God", that only its Maker can master.
readings: Read as natural history

Behemoth is the hippopotamus, drawn by a poet with wonder: its strength, its bones like bronze, its calm in a flooding river. God's point is that he made it "as well as you", and Job cannot even catch it.
Read as myth

Behemoth is a primeval monster, the land counterpart of Leviathan, as later Jewish writings say (1 Enoch 60:7–9; 4 Ezra 6:49–52). God's mastery over it shows his mastery over chaos, the very forces Job felt had been turned against him.
Read as both
The poet paints a real animal larger than life, with the mythic weight it had in Egypt, where the hippo stood for chaos. The beast is real, and it is a sign.

views.H: Readers who take Job as history usually see Behemoth as a real animal known to Job, most often the hippopotamus (or the elephant, in older Christian writers). Some young-earth creationists identify it with a dinosaur that they believe lived alongside humans.
views.C: Critics debate whether the Behemoth and Leviathan poems (40:15–41:34) belong to the original book. Some think the second speech was added because Job's first reply seemed too weak; most now read it as part of the design, with the second speech answering the question of justice that the first leaves open (40:8).
views.W: In Egypt the king or the god Horus harpooning a hippopotamus stood for the victory of order over Seth and chaos; temple reliefs at Edfu show it. Othmar Keel argued that Job 40–41 draws on this picture: God, not the king, is the true master of the chaos beasts.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition makes Behemoth a giant beast that grazes on a thousand hills each day (Psalm 50:10), kept with Leviathan for the feast of the righteous in the world to come (Bava Batra 74b; Leviticus Rabbah 13:3). The medieval poem Akdamut, sung on Shavuot, describes the battle of Leviathan and the great wild ox at the end of days.
views.X: Gregory the Great reads Behemoth as the devil, "the first of the ways of God" because Satan was the greatest angel before his fall. Aquinas gives the literal sense as the elephant and the spiritual sense as the devil. William Blake's engraving "Behold now Behemoth" (1826) shows God showing Job and his wife the two beasts in a globe beneath the earth.

deep.b: Job's first reply (40:3–5) is silence, and God speaks again. The first speech was about the order of creation; the second is about justice. God asks whether Job will "overturn my justice" (40:8) and dares him to do the work of the divine king: pour out anger, humble the proud, bury the wicked (40:10–13). Then God himself will praise Job (40:14). The irony cuts two ways. Job cannot do it, so he should stop accusing God. But the speech also admits that pride and wickedness are real and must be brought down, and that ruling a world with free and fierce creatures in it is not simple. Behemoth and Leviathan then serve as pictures of what God must master and Job cannot.

(1) Hippopotamus: Bochart (1663) and most modern dictionaries; it fits grass, reeds, lotus and river. (2) Elephant: Aquinas, Calvin and many older Christian writers; it fits "first of the ways of God" as the greatest land animal. (3) Mythic monster: Pope, John Day and others, linking it to Ugaritic myth and to Jewish tradition that pairs it with Leviathan. (4) Real animal with mythic meaning: Keel, Habel, Newsom. (5) Dinosaur: young-earth creationists such as Henry Morris, mainly on the strength of the tail like a cedar (40:17); scholars reply that the tail line is a euphemism or poetic exaggeration, and that the river-marsh setting fits the hippo. The text calls it "Behemoth", "the Beast", which leaves it open.

Readers using a Jewish Bible (such as the JPS) or a Hebrew text will find that chapter 40 does not end at verse 24. Hebrew chapter 40 runs on to 40:32, so its 40:25–32 are this site's 41:1–8, and Hebrew 41:1–26 are English 41:9–34. The older Latin Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims number differently again: English 40:1–5 is their 39:31–35, and Behemoth begins at their 40:10. See the note at 41:1.

settings.to: The LORD, who has just challenged him to answer
settings.when: At the end of the first speech from the storm
settings.why: Job admits that he is too small to answer and puts his hand over his mouth, but he does not withdraw his case. His words are meant to end the exchange: he will say nothing more. They do not, because God wants more than silence.
settings.readers: For Israelites after the exile, who knew bold protest prayers such as Psalm 44 and Psalm 88, Job's reply modeled another honest response: not confessing sins one has not done, but falling silent before God's greatness. The book will not let that silence be the last word.
views: Job is humbled and awed (Andersen, Hartley).
Job is silenced but not convinced, which is why a second speech follows (Habel, Clines).

settings.what: The LORD's second speech from the storm
settings.why: God takes up the question of justice: Job has made God guilty to make himself innocent (40:8). God dares Job to rule the world and humble the proud, then shows him two creatures that only God can master, Behemoth and Leviathan. The speech is meant to move Job from silence to real acceptance, and to show that God's justice works on a scale and against powers Job cannot see.
settings.readers: For readers living under Persian or Greek rule, who knew the promise that God would one day punish Leviathan (Isaiah 27:1), the two beasts spoke of powers stronger than any human army, including the empires that had swallowed Israel. The speech told them that God made those powers and holds them on a leash.
views: God silences Job by force of majesty (many readers, some critically).
God shows that the chaos Job feels is God's creature and under his control (Habel, Day, Levenson).
God speaks with pride of creatures Job fears, inviting him to share God's view (Newsom, Alter).

title: Leviathan
sum: The longest description of any creature in the Bible. God asks whether Job can catch Leviathan with a fishhook, make it beg, sign a treaty with it, keep it as a pet or sell it in pieces. One look at it and a hunter falls flat. If no one dares wake it, who can stand against its Maker?

Then God praises the beast's body: double jaws, teeth ringed with dread, rows of shields on its back, sneezes that flash light, smoke from its nostrils and fire from its mouth. Iron is straw to it, the gods fear it, it makes the deep boil and leaves a white wake. "There is nothing like it on all the earth's dust"; it is king of all the proud. The speech ends there, with no conclusion drawn.
readings: Read as the crocodile

Many of the details fit the Nile crocodile: armored scales, terrible teeth, eyes rising at dawn, hunted with hooks and harpoons. The fire and smoke are poetic exaggeration. God boasts of a creature Job cannot touch.
Read as the chaos dragon

Leviathan is the sea monster of Ugaritic and biblical myth (Isaiah 27:1; Psalm 74:14), the seven-headed Lotan of Ugarit. It breathes fire and terrifies gods. God does not fight it here; he describes it as his own creature, which is the boldest claim in the book.
Read as the devil

Many Christian and some Jewish readers see in Leviathan the power of evil, the serpent and dragon of Genesis 3 and Revelation 12. Only God can conquer it; Gregory the Great says Christ caught it on the hook of the cross.

views.H: Readers who take Job as history generally identify Leviathan with a real animal Job could know, most often the crocodile (some older writers: the whale). Some creationists propose a marine reptile or dinosaur. Others in this camp read the fire-breathing lines as poetry.
views.C: Critics note the change in style and length and sometimes judge the poem an addition. Most see it as the climax of the second speech. The Hebrew chapter break falls eight verses later (English 41:9 is Hebrew 41:1), see the note at 41:1. The Old Greek had both beast poems. Rahlfs' text, as displayed on die-bibel.de, carries critical signs at a few lines in 38–41 (38:26–27, 38:32, 40:2, 40:23, and English 41:12 and 41:32), which appear to mark short supplements from Theodotion; their exact extent was not confirmed for this site, so treat this as provisional. The long gap at 39:13–18 is certain.
views.W: In the Ugaritic Baal cycle Mot reminds Baal that he struck down Lotan, "the fleeing serpent... the twisting serpent, the mighty one with seven heads" (KTU 1.5 i 1–3, paraphrased), and Anat claims to have muzzled the dragon Tunnan (KTU 1.3 iii). Isaiah 27:1 uses the same two descriptions for Leviathan. In Babylon Marduk splits the sea-monster Tiamat. Job differs: Leviathan is neither defeated nor feared by God, but admired.
views.J: The Talmud (Bava Batra 74b–75a) says God made Leviathan male and female and killed the female so they would not fill the world, salting her flesh for the righteous; that Gabriel will hunt Leviathan in the future; and that the righteous will feast on it and sit in a booth made of its skin. 1 Enoch, 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch already keep Behemoth and Leviathan for the last days. The prayer on leaving the sukkah asks to sit next year in the sukkah of Leviathan's skin.
views.X: Gregory the Great's Moralia (books 32–34) reads Leviathan as the devil and the fishhook of 41:1 as Christ: the devil swallowed the bait of Christ's human flesh and was caught on the hook of his divinity, an image also used by Gregory of Nyssa (Catechetical Oration 24). Calvin and many Protestants preferred a literal animal (the whale or crocodile). Revelation's dragon, "that ancient serpent" (Revelation 12:9), draws on the same imagery.

deep.b:
Leviathan appears five times. Job cursed his day by calling on those "ready to wake Leviathan" (3:8). Psalm 74:14 says God crushed Leviathan's heads and gave it as food to desert creatures, a picture of God's victory at creation or at the Exodus. Psalm 104:26 says God formed Leviathan to play in the sea. Isaiah 27:1 promises that "on that day" the LORD with his hard, great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and kill the dragon in the sea (a fresh rendering), a future victory over evil powers. Job 41 is unlike all of these: God neither kills nor plays with Leviathan; he praises it, and asks Job to look.

The book has prepared for this. Job asked, "Am I the Sea, or am I the Dragon, that you station a guard over me?" (7:12). Here is the answer: God does guard the sea and the dragon, but Job is not one of them.

deep.title: Claude's reading: Leviathan's pride and Job's
deep.b: This is my reading, though it overlaps with Habel and Newsom. The speech begins by daring Job to "spot every proud one and knock him low" (40:11–12), and ends with a creature that is "king of all the proud" (41:34), whose "pride" is its armor (41:15). God can humble Leviathan; Job cannot. But God does not humble it here. He admires it. If so, God is not asking Job to stop being strong or to despise his own fierce honesty. He is showing Job a pride that God enjoys because it is under his rule, and inviting Job to see his own defiance in the same light: real, even admirable, but not ultimate. That would fit God's verdict that Job spoke what is right (42:7).

echoes: 3:8; 7:12; 26:12–13; Genesis 1:21; Psalm 74:13–14; Psalm 104:26; Isaiah 27:1; Isaiah 51:9; Ezekiel 29:3–5; Romans 11:35; Revelation 12:3; Revelation 12:9; Revelation 13:1

views: The Church has no ruling. Gregory the Great's Moralia, the most influential Catholic reading, takes Leviathan as the devil, caught by Christ; Aquinas keeps that as the spiritual sense but gives the whale as the literal one. Most modern Catholic scholars read a crocodile drawn with the imagery of the mythic sea beast.

The Fathers and the liturgy often read the dragon of the sea as the devil, crushed by Christ in the waters of baptism (Psalm 74:13–14 in the Theophany blessing of the waters); Leviathan in Job is read in that light, without denying the creature.

Calvin preached Leviathan as a real animal (the whale) and drew from it God's power over all creatures, warning against allegory; many Reformed interpreters follow him, while some link the image to Satan through Isaiah 27:1 and Revelation 12.

Divided: some popular teachers identify Leviathan with Satan via Isaiah 27:1 and Revelation 12:9; young-earth creationists read a real sea reptile or dinosaur; most evangelical commentators (Hartley, Andersen) read a crocodile described with mythic imagery.

title: Now My Eye Has Seen You
sum: Job answers the LORD a last time. He knows that God can do anything and that no plan of his can be stopped. Quoting God's own challenges, he admits that he spoke of wonders beyond him. "Before, I had only heard about you, but now my own eye has seen you." And so he takes back what he said and changes his mind about dust and ashes. The Plain follows this retraction reading; repentance, comfort and even rejection of God are the main alternatives, and the verse is one of the most debated sentences in the Bible.

Then the prose story returns. The LORD is furious with Eliphaz and his two friends, "You did not say what is right about me, the way my servant Job did." They must offer a great sacrifice, and Job must pray for them. When Job prays for his friends, the LORD turns his life around and doubles all he had. His family comes to comfort him. He has seven sons and three daughters, Jemimah, Keziah and Keren-happuch, the most beautiful women in the land, who inherit alongside their brothers. Job lives a hundred and forty more years and dies old and satisfied with days.
readings: Read as repentance and reward

Job repents of his rash words, and God, satisfied, restores him. This is the traditional reading, and it fits the shape of a story of testing (Abraham in Genesis 22; James 5:11, which speaks of "the outcome from the Lord").
Read as vindication

The key line is 42:7: God says Job spoke rightly, and the friends did not. Job's honest protest is accepted; the friends' defense of God is condemned. The restoration is not a reward for repenting but a public declaration that Job was in the right.
Read as a problem

Many modern readers find the happy ending too neat. New children do not replace dead ones, and the doubled flocks seem to return to the very idea of reward the poem undermined. Some (Newsom) see the clash between poem and prose as deliberate: the book refuses to let any one voice have the last word.

views.H: Readers who take Job as history accept the restoration and long life as fact, and many place Job in the patriarchal age because of the numbers and the phrase "old and satisfied with days". The Greek ending (see the variant at 42:17) makes him Jobab king of Edom.
views.C: Most critics see the prose epilogue (42:7–17) as part of an older folk tale, kept by the poet as the frame. They note that it says nothing of Elihu or of the Accuser, that God's praise of Job (42:7) fits the patient Job of the prologue better than the angry Job of the poem, and that the poet may have kept the tension on purpose.
views.W: The Babylonian poem I Will Praise the Lord of Wisdom (Ludlul) ends with the sufferer healed and restored by Marduk, and the Sumerian Man and His God ends with the god turning the man's suffering to joy. In the Ugaritic tale of Kirta, a king who has lost his whole family is given a new one by the god El. Job's ending belongs to this pattern, but only Job has a God who declares the sufferer's complaint right and his comforters wrong.
views.J: The Talmud (Bava Batra 16b) explains the daughters' names: Jemimah was fair as the day (yom), Keziah had the fragrance of cassia. Maimonides (Guide 3.23) says Job's change in 42:6 came from true knowledge of God, which replaced the mere tradition he had before (42:5). Some rabbis said Job served God out of love, others out of fear; the debate turns on these chapters (Mishnah Sotah 5:5).
views.X: James 5:11 holds up Job's endurance and "the outcome from the Lord", that the Lord is full of compassion and mercy. Gregory the Great, who reads Job throughout as a figure of Christ, sees in Job's prayer for his friends a picture of Christ interceding for sinners. Kierkegaard's Repetition (1843) makes Job's getting "everything double" a picture of receiving the world back as a gift. The Orthodox Church reads the Greek ending, with its hope that Job "will rise again".

deep.h: What 42:7 does to the whole debate
deep.b:
For thirty-five chapters the friends defended God's justice: the righteous prosper and the wicked suffer, so Job must have sinned (4:7–8; 8:3–6; 11:6; 22:5). Job insisted on his innocence and accused God of injustice (9:22–24; 19:6–7; 27:2). A reader schooled in Proverbs or Deuteronomy would expect God to side with the friends. Instead God says twice that they "did not say what is right" about him, "the way my servant Job did" (42:7–8).

This changes how the whole debate must be read. (1) Defending God with false claims is a sin; Job warned them, "Is it for God that you speak what is unjust?" (13:7). (2) The simple rule of reward and punishment is not a full account of God's ways, even though God does bless Job in the end. (3) Honest complaint addressed to God is acceptable to him, perhaps more than pious talk about him; the Hebrew elay may mean "to me" as well as "about me". (4) Job is not declared sinless; God has rebuked his words (38:2; 40:8). What he said that was "right" may be his insistence that he did not deserve this, which the prologue confirms (1:8; 2:3). Readers differ on whether "what is right" covers all of Job's words or only his final ones, but on any reading the friends' theology loses.

deep.h: Job's last words: repentance, comfort or retraction
deep.b:
Job 42:6 has five Hebrew words, and three of them can be read more than one way (see the three notes on the verse). The Plain's choice. The Plain follows the retraction reading: em'as "I reject", with "what I said" supplied from 42:3; nichamti 'al as the set phrase "change one's mind about" (Exodus 32:14; Amos 7:3); and "dust and ashes" left as the Hebrew has it, meaning either the mourning Job sat in (2:8) or the human lot (30:19; Genesis 18:27). Pope, Patrick, Habel, Morrow and the 1985 JPS read the verse this way.

Repentance. "I despise myself and repent in dust and ashes" (KJV). Its evidence: ma'as stands without an object for Job's own life in 7:16 and 9:21; nicham 'al means "repent of" in Jeremiah 8:6; the Vulgate reads "I rebuke myself and do penance in embers and ashes"; and 11QtgJob ends "and I shall become dust and ashes". Rashi, Calvin, Andersen and Hartley hold it. Comfort. Nicham 'al can mean "be comforted about" (2 Samuel 13:39): Clines, "I submit, and I accept consolation for my dust and ashes"; Greenstein, "I take pity on dust and ashes"; Mitchell. Melting. The Greek "I despised myself and melted" and 11QtgJob "I am poured out and dissolved" read a root "melt". Rejection. Curtis: Job rejects God and is sorry for frail humanity. Newsom argues that the poet left the ambiguity on purpose.

echoes: Genesis 18:27; Genesis 20:7; Genesis 25:8; Genesis 35:29; Genesis 36:33; Numbers 23:1; Numbers 27:7–8; Deuteronomy 30:3; Psalm 126:4; Ezekiel 14:14; James 5:11; 1:2–3; 2:11; 13:7–10; 19:13–14; 19:25–27

settings.to: The LORD, after the second speech from the storm
settings.when: At the end of the speeches, before the prose ending
settings.why: Job confesses God's power and freedom, admits he spoke beyond his knowledge, and says that his hearing of God has become seeing. Then he takes back what he said and changes his mind about dust and ashes (the Plain's retraction reading; others read repentance, comfort or rejection). The words end Job's part in the dialogue and prepare for God's verdict.
settings.readers: Readers who had learned the great confessions of sin after the exile (Ezra 9; Nehemiah 9) found here a different model for coming before God: neither the friends' easy answers nor endless accusation, but telling God the truth, meeting him, and letting go of the demand to understand.
views: Job withdraws his words and his case (the Plain; Pope, Patrick, Habel, Morrow, JPS).
Job repents of rash words (tradition; Rashi, Calvin, Andersen, Hartley).
Job accepts consolation as a mortal (Clines, Mitchell, Greenstein; Newsom sees deliberate ambiguity).
Job rejects God and pities humankind (Curtis).

settings.what: The LORD's verdict on the friends
settings.to: Eliphaz the Temanite, for himself and his two friends (Bildad and Zophar); Elihu is not mentioned
settings.when: Right after the speeches to Job
settings.why: God condemns the friends for not speaking what is right about him, praises Job twice as "my servant", and orders a great burnt offering with Job as the one who prays for them. The verdict reverses the debate: the defenders of God are guilty, the accuser of God is vindicated, and the man they called a sinner becomes their priest.
settings.readers: For readers who had been told that their sufferings proved their sins, the verdict was a defense. It warned the comforters of every age that false theology is a sin against God, and it told the suffering that honest prayer is not rebellion.
views: Job spoke truthfully about his experience (Clines, Newsom).
The friends' rule of reward and punishment was false (Maimonides; Habel).
Only Job's last replies are meant (some traditional readers).

settings.by: The narrator of the prose frame
settings.when: After the friends' sacrifice and Job's prayer
settings.why: The story closes as it began, in prose: Job's fortunes are turned back, his goods doubled, his family and friends gather, ten children are born, the daughters are named and given an inheritance, and Job dies full of years. The ending shows that God's verdict in favor of Job was real and public.
settings.readers: For a community that had prayed, "LORD, turn our fortunes back again" (Psalm 126:4), the Hebrew phrase behind "turned Job's fortunes around" (42:10), literally "turned back his captivity", was the prophets' promise of return from exile (Deuteronomy 30:3; Jeremiah 29:14). The ending held out hope that God would turn their fortunes too, without pretending that the losses had not happened.
views: The restoration declares Job in the right (Clines, Habel).
The happy ending sits uneasily with the poem, perhaps on purpose (Newsom).

traditions.q: Is the Greek ending of Job (42:17a–e), with its hope that Job "will rise again", part of Scripture?
views: Yes, as part of the Septuagint text of Job, which the Orthodox Church receives as its Old Testament; its line that Job "will rise again" is read as a witness to the resurrection.
No. The Catholic canon includes Job as found in the Hebrew and the Vulgate, which lack the ending; the Council of Trent defined the canon "as found in the old Latin Vulgate".
No. Protestant Bibles follow the Hebrew text, and the ending is treated as a later Greek addition with no authority as Scripture (Westminster Confession 1.2–3, 1.8).
